title: A 170km Fiber Link Just Beat the Diffraction Limit by 4x
hook: Borrowing phase-stabilization tricks from quantum communications, physicists turned a 170km optical fiber into an interferometer sharp enough to beat the diffraction limit by 4x.
key_points: Any telescope's resolution is capped by the diffraction limit, set by the wavelength observed and the size of its aperture — bigger apertures see finer detail.
Linking distant telescopes via interferometry synthesizes a much larger effective aperture, but long optical fiber links are highly sensitive to phase noise from the fiber itself.
Researchers adapted phase-stabilization techniques from quantum communications to tame that noise over a 170km fiber pseudo-baseline.

Using a quantum-optimal measurement technique, they resolved a source four times smaller than the system's diffraction limit, with only 1.5% error — a step toward a full-scale 350km interferometer that could resolve sub-microarcsecond features.
content_html: Every telescope has a hard resolution ceiling called the diffraction limit — set by the light's wavelength and the telescope's aperture size. Astronomers get around this by linking multiple telescopes together as an interferometer, effectively synthesizing a much bigger aperture. Doing that over free-space beams is one thing; doing it over long stretches of optical fiber is another, because the fiber medium itself introduces phase noise that scrambles the delicate signal interferometry depends on.
extra_html: A team led by Joshua J. Collier and David R. Gozzard adapted phase-stabilization techniques developed for quantum communications to tame that noise over an unusually long 170km fiber pseudo-baseline. Combined with a quantum-optimal measurement technique, their interferometer resolved the extent of a source four times smaller than the system's diffraction limit, with just 1.5% error. It's a proof-of-principle result rather than an astronomical observation, but it brings a full-scale, on-sky long-baseline optical interferometer meaningfully closer — the team estimates a 350km version at 1550nm could resolve features smaller than a millionth of an arcsecond across the sky.

flashcards.prompt: What sets the resolution limit of any single telescope?
flashcards.back_html: The diffraction limit — determined by the wavelength of light observed and the size of the telescope's aperture. Bigger apertures resolve finer detail.

flashcards.prompt: Why are fiber-linked interferometers harder to build than free-space ones over long distances?

choices.text: Optical fiber is much more susceptible to phase noise from inhomogeneities in the fiber medium
Fiber cables cannot carry light at astronomically useful wavelengths
Fiber links can only work over distances shorter than 1 km

flashcards.explanation_html: Inhomogeneities inside the fiber degrade the phase signal needed for interferometry, an effect that gets worse as the fiber baseline lengthens.

flashcards.prompt: What result did the team achieve with their 170km fiber pseudo-baseline?
flashcards.back_html: They resolved a source four times smaller than the system's diffraction limit, with just 1.5% error — using phase-stabilization techniques borrowed from quantum communications.
